title: The Easter Octave
hookLine: eight days counted as one great day

cards: Most parties end when the guests go home. By Tuesday it's just Tuesday. The Church does something odd with Easter.
On Monday the Gloria is sung again. On Tuesday, again. All week the prayers at Mass keep saying this day, today, as if the sun hadn't set, and the dismissal still ends with a double alleluia.
In parts of Europe, Easter Monday is a public holiday, and the visiting goes on. The calendar refuses to turn the page.

teach.b: An octave comes from the Latin octava, the eighth.
In the calendar, it means a feast kept for eight days, from the day itself to the same weekday a week later.

The Church's rules say it plainly: the first eight days of the Easter season make up the octave of Easter and are celebrated as solemnities of the Lord. Every one of them outranks almost anything else.

That's why, in the Church's daily prayer, the Liturgy of the Hours, the Easter line from the Psalm, This is the day which the Lord hath made, comes back at every hour all week. It isn't eight Easters.
It's one great day stretched across eight. Why eight? Early Christians noticed that Jesus rose on the first day of the week, which is also the day after the seventh: the eighth day.

The Epistle of Barnabas and Justin Martyr call Sunday the eighth day, the start of a new creation beyond the old week. Some old baptismal fonts have eight sides, and some readers see the same idea there.
And tradition says the newly baptized from the Vigil wore their white garments through this week. The octave ends next Sunday.
Only two octaves remain in the Roman calendar now, Christmas and Easter.

teach.h: THIS IS THE DAY WHICH THE LORD HATH MADE.
teach.b: And this closes week ninety-five: the oils blessed at the Chrism Mass, the washing of feet on Holy Thursday, the wood of the cross on Good Friday, the waiting of Holy Saturday, the whole story at the Vigil, the empty tomb, and now one long day.

how: During the Easter octave Catholics celebrate each day from Easter Sunday to the following Sunday as a solemnity, with the Gloria at Mass and a double alleluia at the dismissal; in many countries Easter Monday is a public holiday.

games.q: it's Thursday after Easter. a big saint's feast falls on that date. what happens at Mass?
o: Easter Thursday is celebrated; the saint gives way.
games.why: the octave days are solemnities of the Lord and outrank almost everything. the feast is moved or skipped that year.

practice: Pick one small thing from Sunday you could repeat each day until next Sunday: a candle at dinner, one alleluia at the door, a flower on the table, a piece of chocolate saved for each evening. Hold it in mind, small enough to keep.
If you pray, you can say the Gloria, or just the line this is the day the Lord hath made.

wordCard.voice: Octave. From the Latin for eighth: a feast kept for eight days as one. Easter's octave runs from Sunday to Sunday. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: the eighth; a feast kept for eight days.

carryVoice: Your line: one long day. Eight days, one Easter, and the page still hasn't turned. Day six hundred sixty-five.
